## 1. Introduction: VIGÍA and the New Frontier of Forensic Intent Analysis

### 1.1 The Problem: Limitations of Traditional DFIR

On February 22, 2026, Rob T. Lee, Chief AI Officer of the SANS Institute, spoke two words to his laptop at RSAC: *find evil*. Fourteen minutes and twenty-seven seconds later, an autonomous agent built on SIFT Workstation had completed a forensic analysis of a C: drive that, according to incident responders, usually takes a week or more [^42^]. That demonstration wasn't just a technical feat — it was a brutal diagnosis of a profession in crisis.

Traditional **DFIR** (*Digital Forensics and Incident Response*) has operated for decades under an insufficient paradigm: it asks *what* happened, but rarely *why* the evidence looks the way it does. When an analyst examines logs or memory processes, they interpret artifacts without interrogating the deliberate decisions that produced them. That omission isn't academic — it's structurally exploitable.

The crisis shows up in stark numbers. CrowdStrike's *Global Threat Report 2026* reveals that **82% of 2025 detections were malware-free** — attacks that operated exclusively through **LotL** techniques (*Living Off the Land*, using legitimate system tools for malicious ends) [^838^]. The *Picus Blue Report 2025* confirms that organizations detect barely **1 in 7 simulated attacks** (~14%) [^810^]. *Breakout time* — between infiltration and lateral movement — has dropped to **29 minutes**, with a record of 27 seconds [^836^].

Behind these numbers lies the **EDR trust crisis** (*Endpoint Detection and Response*). Commercial EDRs operate as **black boxes** — opaque machine-learning models, non-deterministic floating thresholds, and an inability to explain their classifications — which makes them vulnerable to evasion and judicial exclusion [^769^]. A DEF CON 32 study found that **94% of the EDR solutions analyzed lack hooks at the layer above NTDLL**, leaving a systemic architectural gap [^821^]. EDR evasion has become a **commodity**: tools like AuKill and EDRKillShifter sell for **$300** on underground forums [^782^], while LACUNA Chain demonstrated a full call-stack-based detection bypass in June 2026 [^799^].

**Anti-forensic** techniques have evolved from log wiping to sophisticated artifact fabrication. **APT** (*Advanced Persistent Threat*) groups like Lazarus and Sandworm don't just hide evidence — they plant it to deceive [^822^][^783^]. The **Olympic Destroyer** case (2018) encapsulates this reality: Russian attackers imitated Lazarus's TTPs (*Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures*) so convincingly that investigators initially attributed the attack to North Korea [^783^]. When the evidence itself lies, asking only *what* happened is no longer enough.

| Metric | Value | Source |
|---------|-------|--------|
| Malware-free detections (2025) | 82% | CrowdStrike GTR 2026 [^838^] |
| Undetected simulated attacks | ~86% (6/7) | Picus Blue Report 2025 [^810^] |
| Average breakout time | 29 minutes | CrowdStrike GTR 2026 [^836^] |
| Minimum EDR-killer price | $300 USD | Underground forums [^782^] |
| EDRs blind above NTDLL | 94% | DEF CON 32 [^821^] |
| AI-enabled attacks (YoY) | +89% | CrowdStrike GTR 2026 [^835^] |

### 1.2 VIGÍA: Vision and Value Proposition

**VIGÍA** (*Virtual Intent-Guided Inference Analyzer*) is a deterministic abductive-inference engine that evaluates **the logical fractures in a lie**. Its founding principle: *Today, lying in a log or faking an attack is free. VIGÍA charges that price by evaluating the logical fractures in the lie* [^853^].

The key architectural distinction is **LLM isolation** from the verdict pipeline: *verdicts are sealed before any LLM* (*Large Language Model*) *ever sees the evidence*. The engine runs exclusively on integer arithmetic using `fractions.Fraction` and SHA-256 for integrity; LLMs participate only in post-verdict narrative. This design responds to an empirical lesson: the **BREAK-012** case documented how an LLM incorrectly flipped a verdict from BENIGN to MALICE after accessing data before sealing [^854^].

VIGÍA measures **spoofability** — how easy each evidence type is to fake. IP geolocation has a *spoofability* of 0.90 (easily faked); a memory process has 0.15 (structurally irrefutable) [^853^]. The operating philosophy is summed up as: **make deception computationally expensive for the attacker** [^853^]. *Indicators of Intent* (**IoI**) replace the traditional *Indicators of Compromise* (**IoC**).

| Dimension | Traditional DFIR | VIGÍA |
|-----------|-----------------|-------|
| **Central question** | What happened? | Why does the evidence look this way? Who benefits? |
| **Unit of analysis** | IoC (hash, IP, signature) | IoI (intentional inconsistency, narrative fracture) |
| **LotL detection** | Limited — requires behavioral signatures | Native — "known processes doing unknown things" [^853^] |
| **False-flag resistance** | Low — correlates isolated artifacts | High — CAIE detects cross-artifact incongruence [^853^] |
| **Determinism** | Not guaranteed | Guaranteed bit-for-bit — `fractions.Fraction` + SHA-256 [^853^] |
| **Transparency** | Black-box EDRs, proprietary algorithms | Apache 2.0 open source, stdlib-only verifier |
| **Offline mode** | Reduced functionality | 0-token mode — full operation with no LLM or internet [^225^] |
| **Philosophy under uncertainty** | Force a binary classification | ABSTAIN as a valid, epistemologically correct verdict [^854^] |

### 1.3 Development Context

VIGÍA was built for the **SANS FIND EVIL Hackathon 2026**, the first autonomous-agent DFIR hackathon, with 4,178+ participants and $22,000 USD in prizes [^40^][^41^]. The challenge: turn **Protocol SIFT** — Rob T. Lee's initiative to connect LLMs to 500+ forensic tools via Anthropic's **MCP** (*Model Context Protocol*) [^55^] — into an autonomous DFIR agent capable of thinking like a senior analyst and self-correcting [^41^].

The project was led by **Anna Tchijova**, a professional cook of Russian origin living in Argentina with no formal IT training, who orchestrated an **AI Collective** of 7 LLMs with specialized roles: Claude (integration), Gemini (IoI theoretical framework), Kimi (forensic systems), DeepSeek (security audit), Qwen (hardening), Grok (scoring architecture), and ChatGPT (adversarial red team) [^222^][^225^]. Development followed cycles of debate, code writing, and competitive auditing between models [^225^].

This report investigates the *vigia-intent-analysis* repository, synthesizing findings across 10 independent dimensions, 250+ web searches, source-code analysis, and a review of academic literature in philosophy of science, semiotics, artificial intelligence, digital forensics, and law.

> *Example case — CAN-031: Weaponized Incompetence.* An actor runs PowerShell to delete *shadow copies* and disable the firewall with zero syntax errors. Sixty-three seconds later, they file an IT ticket: "my screen flickered, I'm useless with computers." A traditional investigator sees accidental incompetence. VIGÍA detects the fracture: the absence of errors in destructive commands contradicts the incompetence narrative, and the 63-second timing is statistically anomalous. **CAIE** (*Cross-Artifact Incongruence Engine*) computes the discrepancy between flawless technical behavior and a feigned narrative, raising the verdict to MALICE [^853^].

This report examines how VIGÍA transforms digital forensics from a cataloguing discipline into deterministic intentional inference — and why that transition is mandatory in a landscape where 82% of threats leave no malware trace and EDR killers cost less than a movie ticket.

## 2. Theoretical Foundations: From Peircean Abductive Reasoning to Forensic Semiotics

### 2.1 Charles Sanders Peirce and the Three Ontological Categories

#### 2.1.1 Firstness, Secondness, Thirdness Applied to Digital Evidence

Charles Sanders Peirce (1839–1914) built his philosophical system on three mutually irreducible phenomenological categories: Firstness, Secondness, and Thirdness. This ontological framework underpins his entire semiotics and his logic of scientific discovery [^1^], and constitutes the foundation on which VIGÍA erects its inference architecture — not as metaphor, but as an executable data structure [^2^].

Firstness designates pure quality, unmediated immediacy. Peirce defines it as that whose being "is simply in itself... a kind of unmediated meditative state without unity and without parts, it just 'is'" [^3^]. Relationally, it corresponds to monadic predicates — properties an entity possesses without reference to anything else [^4^]. In digital forensics, Firstness manifests in raw data: a timestamp, a hash, a registry entry. These are digital *qualia* that exist as mere presence prior to any interpretation.

Secondness is the category of fact, existence, resistance: "the knock on the door which interrupts the musical reverie; it is the unexpected rear-end collision" [^5^]. Relationally, it corresponds to dyadic predicates requiring two correlates: action-reaction, cause-effect [^4^]. In digital evidence, Secondness emerges when two artifacts enter into relation — one timestamp contradicts another, a process record is inconsistent with a network log, volatile memory refutes the persistent-storage narrative.

Thirdness is the category of law, habit, mediation. Peirce illustrates it: "Tycho Brahe's recorded observations of the positions of the planet Mars at given times are seconds. Kepler's laws, worked out to unify that body of data, are thirds" [^6^]. Relationally, it requires triadic predicates — subject, object, interpretant — in an act of semiosis [^4^]. In digital forensics, Thirdness corresponds to the explanatory hypothesis that unifies incongruent artifacts: the attribution of intent, the reconstruction of the attack chain.

Peirce held that Thirdness is strictly irreducible: "I will sketch a proof that the idea of meaning is irreducible to those of quality and reaction... a triadic relation is inexpressible by means of dyadic relations alone" [^7^]. This thesis has direct consequences for inference-system architecture: an explanatory hypothesis cannot be reduced to the sum of data plus its correlations, which justifies an abduction engine as an independent component.

**Diagram 2.1: Peirce–VIGÍA Ontological Hierarchy (text description)**

The diagram depicts a three-level pyramid with inclusion arrows indicating irreducibility. At the base (Level 1), Firstness is shown as isolated hexagonal nodes labeled *Artifact* (timestamp, hash, registry entry). At the middle level (Level 2), Secondness appears as dyadic arrows labeled *CAIE* connecting pairs of lower-level nodes — for example, *timestamp_A* to *timestamp_B* under the label *TEMPORAL_CAUSALITY_VIOLATION*. At the apex (Level 3), Thirdness materializes as an *AbductiveHypothesis* ellipse that groups Level-2 arrows under a unifying narrative (e.g., *log_fabrication*). Dashed arrows descending from Thirdness indicate that the hypothesis generates testable predictions via the *what_would_falsify* field. Diagonal bars labeled "irreducible" block the reduction of Level 3 to Level 2+1, materializing Peirce's thesis on the irreducibility of triadicity.

#### 2.1.2 The Inferential Triad: Abduction, Deduction, Induction in Forensic Investigation

Peirce held that complete scientific inquiry requires three mutually irreducible inferences. Abduction adopts an explanatory hypothesis in the face of surprising facts; deduction derives its observable consequences; induction subjects them to empirical testing [^8^]. The forensic investigator reproduces this cycle: they observe an anomalous artifact, formulate an attack scenario, predict what evidence would corroborate that scenario, and check those predictions against the available corpus [^9^].

| Inferential Phase | Peircean Definition | Forensic Implementation | Function in VIGÍA |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Abduction** | Suggesting a hypothesis that explains the observation [^8^] | Generating explanatory hypotheses from anomalous artifacts | `AbductiveIntentEngine.infer()` — produces hypotheses with required and assumed artifacts |
| **Deduction** | Tracing the probable experiential consequences [^8^] | Specifying falsification conditions | `what_would_falsify` field — predicts data that would invalidate the hypothesis |
| **Induction** | Experimental testing of the hypothesis [^8^] | Empirical evaluation via integer scoring and active falsification | Scoring engine + Devil's Advocate — inductive verification against evidence |

The table synthesizes the Peircean inferential triad alongside its VIGÍA implementation. The `what_would_falsify` field provides the deductive mechanism for ruling out alternatives; the *Devil's Advocate* closes the loop with counter-arguments that can restart abduction. This triadic integrity is epistemologically critical: a system that only generates hypotheses without specifying falsification conditions lacks scientific rigor; one that only tests without generating new hypotheses is purely confirmatory.

### 2.3 Lorenzo Magnani and Abductive Cognition

#### 2.3.1 Theoretical vs. Manipulative Abduction in Magnani's Framework

Lorenzo Magnani (University of Pavia) developed the most widely cited systematic extension of contemporary Peircean abduction. His monograph *Abductive Cognition* (2009), with 757 citations on Google Scholar, forms the theoretical bridge between classical semiotics and computational architectures [^10^].

Magnani distinguishes two fundamental forms. Theoretical abduction aims at "selecting and creating a set of hypotheses that are able to dispense good (preferred) explanations of data" [^11^], and subdivides into sentential (propositional) and model-based (non-sentential internal representations). Manipulative abduction captures "the role of action in many interesting situations: action provides otherwise unavailable information that enables the agent to solve problems by starting and performing a suitable abductive process" [^11^]. In Magnani's own terms: "Manipulative abduction happens when we are thinking through doing and not only, in a pragmatic sense, about doing" [^12^]. A key concept is the epistemic mediator: external objects — diagrams, instruments, computational data structures — that, when actively manipulated, reveal properties inaccessible to purely theoretical abduction [^11^].

#### 2.3.2 Harman and Lipton's "Inference to the Best Explanation" as Foundation

The contemporary formulation of abduction as *Inference to the Best Explanation* (IBE) comes from Gilbert Harman (1965): the inference "from the fact that a certain hypothesis would explain the evidence, to the truth of that hypothesis" [^13^]. Peter Lipton developed this theory in *Inference to the Best Explanation* (1991; 2nd ed. 2004), introducing the distinction between the *loveliest explanation* — the one providing the most understanding — and the *likeliest explanation* — the most probable one [^14^]. Lipton argued that "the explanation that would, if true, provide the deepest understanding is the explanation that is likeliest to be true" [^14^], identifying the "explanatory virtues" that characterize the best explanation: mechanism, precision, scope, simplicity, fertility, and unification [^15^].

The most cited objection to IBE comes from Bas van Fraassen: the inference only concludes that a hypothesis is the "best of a bad lot," not that it's true [^16^]. Lipton replied that IBE only recommends the winning hypothesis if it's "good enough" [^17^]; Schupbach (2014) considered the objection "misguided" for conflating the purpose of the inference [^18^]. VIGÍA answers computationally via the `what_would_falsify` field, which sets a sufficiency criterion independent of comparison with alternatives, and via the *Devil's Advocate*, which actively explores the space of unformulated hypotheses.

### 2.4 Application to VIGÍA: Computational Semiotics

#### 2.4.1 Materializing Peirce in Python Classes

VIGÍA implements Peirce's three ontological categories as data structures with explicit philosophical correspondence. `Artifact` materializes Firstness — raw forensic data with no interpretation. CAIE (*Cross-Artifact Incongruence Engine*) implements Secondness — dyadic relations between artifacts that detect incongruities. `AbductiveHypothesis` concretizes Thirdness — the explanatory narrative that unifies artifacts through intent attribution [^19^]. The scoring engine implements IBE deterministically: `scored.sort(key=lambda h: (h.cost, -h.coverage_score))` selects the hypothesis with the lowest cost (fewest unobserved assumptions, an operationalized Ockham's razor) and the highest coverage (most data explained) [^20^]. The Magnanian distinction also has an architectural correlate: the `_score_hypothesis()` engine operates sententially; `AbductiveHypothesis` classes contain internal models (model-based); the *Devil's Advocate* and CAIE implement manipulative abduction by actively transforming the hypothesis structure during inference [^21^].

#### 2.4.2 Grice's Maxims Applied to Forensic Evidence

H. Paul Grice (1975) proposed the Cooperative Principle with four maxims: Quantity (give the information required), Quality (don't say what's false), Relation (be relevant), and Manner (avoid obscurity) [^22^]. Hobbs established the connection to abduction: "an implicature can be viewed as an abductive move for the sake of achieving the best interpretation" [^23^]. In digital forensics, a Quantity violation shows up as either excessively detailed logs (*staging*) or insufficient information (*tampering*). A Quality violation emerges when timestamps mutually contradict each other or records lack corroboration. VIGÍA detects these violations operationally: `coverage_score` measures Quantity; CAIE detects inconsistencies (Quality); pattern-matching measures Relation; and the detection of *excessive digital perfection* identifies suspiciously tidy evidence (Manner) [^24^].

#### 2.4.3 Forensic Semiotics as an Emerging Discipline

The convergence of semiotics and digital forensics is consolidating an interdisciplinary academic field. Leone analyzed forensic artifacts as Peircean triadic signs with iconic, indexical, and symbolic dimensions [^25^]. Danesi systematized forensic semiotics, arguing that "semiotics and crime detection are 'two sides of the same cognitive (inference-based) coin'... clues are signs that require interpretation" [^26^]. Crispino proposes reforming forensic science from its foundations: "a trace is not merely a tangible object; it is a sign that requires recognition and interpretation... Peirce's semiotics enhances this quantitative methodology by incorporating the examination of meanings and contexts into the evaluation of the probative value of forensic evidence" [^27^], emphasizing that "all inferences are interpretive... without incorporating the human element, technical quality alone is inadequate" [^28^]. Sorensen, Thellefsen, and Thellefsen have analyzed clues as information and the "semiotic gap" in investigative processes [^29^]. VIGÍA sits in this context as the first computational implementation, at scale, of these principles: every `Artifact` is a Peircean sign, every `AbductiveHypothesis` is an interpretant, and the engine as a whole constitutes a machine of forensic semiosis that operates under explicit semiotic principles rather than ad-hoc heuristics.

## 3. Technical Architecture and Inference Engine

### 3.1 System Structure

#### 3.1.1 Modular Organization

VIGÍA is organized into six functional modules reflecting a separation of responsibilities aligned with the incident-response lifecycle: `engine/` houses the inferential core; `vigia/` contains the intent-analysis components, including `abductive_intent_engine.py` (~1,133 lines) and `core/decision_layer.py`; `forensics/` manages evidence acquisition and preservation; `evidence/` implements the HMAC-SHA256 chain of custody; `models/` defines the immutable data structures (EBS v1); and `governance/` specifies the P2 determinism protocol. This division isn't merely cosmetic: the `models/` module operates under the absolute rule "This module contains DATA ONLY" [^1^], stripping all business logic out of the immutable layer and guaranteeing that evidence bundles remain interpretable without executing production code.

#### 3.1.2 Core Components

The four components that make up the critical pipeline are: *AbductiveIntentEngine* (hypothesis generation and selection engine), *CAIE* (*Cross-Artifact Incongruence Engine*, forensic-fracture detector), *Devil's Advocate* (deterministic abductive-falsification generator), and *DecisionLayer* (verdict arbitration layer). The relationship among them follows a strictly sequential flow: the engine proposes, CAIE checks cross-source coherence, the Devil's Advocate attempts to refute, and the decision layer issues the final verdict. Below, their functions, theoretical grounding, and source files are compared.

| Component | Main Function | Theoretical Foundation | Source File | Lines (approx.) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| AbductiveIntentEngine | Generate and select hypotheses by cost/coverage | Peircean semiotics + Ockham's Razor | `abductive_intent_engine.py` | ~1,133 |
| CAIE | Detect fractures between cross-artifacts | Information theory + Golden Forensic Rules | `tools/caie.py` | ~1,800 |
| Devil's Advocate (R7) | Compose deterministic abductive falsifications | Eco's Razor (abductive falsification) | `core/devil_advocate_gen.py` | ~200 |
| DecisionLayer | 4–8 state arbitration with Fraction thresholds | Contrastive inference (Lipton) + Daubert criterion | `core/decision_layer.py` | ~300 |

The asymmetry in module size is significant. CAIE, at ~1,800 lines, is the largest component because it must evaluate 17 evidence profiles and 9 fracture rules against every candidate hypothesis. By contrast, the Devil's Advocate (~200 lines) operates under the deliberate constraint of "No LLM on this path" [^2^], delegating narrative complexity to a later layer. This distribution reflects a central design principle: determinism is achieved through containment, not expansion.

#### 3.1.3 Pipeline Flow

The full pipeline is described as a five-stage sequence. First, forensic artifacts are encapsulated as `Artifact` instances, each with an identifier ("A001", "A002"), a category (`VariableCategory`: temporal, process, network, persistence, auth, data, evasion, ioc), and an observed value. Second, `AbductiveIntentEngine.infer()` loads the hypothesis templates corresponding to the detected MITRE phase and computes the Ockham cost and coverage for each candidate. Third, CAIE evaluates fractures among the artifacts supporting the leading hypothesis by applying the *Golden Forensic Rules* and adjusts scores via the formula `adjusted_score = raw_score * (1 - spoofability) * weight` [^3^]. Fourth, the Devil's Advocate generates a falsification narrative based on missing signals from the *CasePatternLibrary*. Fifth, `RiskBoundedDecisionLayer` classifies the result into one of four levels (LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, CRITICAL) using thresholds defined as exact Python fractions: `Fraction(15, 100)`, `Fraction(30, 100)`, `Fraction(60, 100)` [^4^].

### 3.2 The Abductive Engine: AbductiveIntentEngine

#### 3.2.1 An Operationalized Ockham's Razor

The engine implements Peircean abduction as a three-phase phenomenological computational process: *Firstness* (the raw observed data, materialized in the `Artifact` class), *Secondness* (the correlations between artifacts, evaluated by CAIE), and *Thirdness* (the explanatory law or habit, instantiated in `AbductiveHypothesis`) [^5^]. The selection of the winning hypothesis operates under Ockham's Razor translated into a computable metric: *cost* is defined as the number of unobserved assumptions (`len(missing_required) + len(assumed_artifacts)`), and *coverage* as the integer percentage of required artifacts actually observed (`(len(observed_required) * 100) // len(required_artifacts)`) [^6^].

The sorting algorithm is deterministic and uses a lexicographic tuple: `scored.sort(key=lambda h: (h.cost, -h.coverage_score))` [^7^]. This single line encapsulates the engine's entire logic: first minimize cost (unobserved assumptions), and in case of a tie, maximize coverage (data explained). The absence of floating point isn't accidental. The docstring comment states: "Ockham cost = integer count (not float). Coverage = integer percentage (not float)" [^8^]. This design decision eliminates the numerical drift that affects systems based on IEEE-754 floating-point arithmetic, whose limitations were exposed in incidents like the Pentium FDIV bug ($475 million), the Patriot missile (28 dead), and the Ariane 5 rocket ($370 million).

#### 3.2.2 The 32 Hypothesis Templates Across 11 MITRE ATT&CK Phases

The engine has 32 hypothesis templates distributed across 11 phases of the MITRE ATT&CK framework. Each template defines the required artifacts, the assumed artifacts (which raise the cost if unobserved), the intent type, and an explicit falsification criterion (`what_would_falsify`), the latter critical for Daubert admissibility on testability grounds. The distribution isn't uniform: the phases most prevalent in real incidents (PERSISTENCE, DEFENSE_EVASION, CREDENTIAL_ACCESS) get 3 templates each, while LATERAL_MOVEMENT and EXFILTRATION get 1 each, reflecting the cross-cutting nature of those techniques. The DISCOVERY and CLEANUP phases have no templates of their own; the former is inherently cross-cutting across all the others, and the latter is post-incident.

#### 3.2.3 Integer Scoring: Fraction Arithmetic for Absolute Determinism

Bit-for-bit determinism is achieved through three interconnected mechanisms. The abductive engine uses exclusively integer arithmetic for all scoring calculations. The decision layer's thresholds use `fractions.Fraction`, which represents exact rationals with no loss of precision: `HIGH_CONFIDENCE_THRESHOLD = Fraction(4, 5)` (80%) and `MEDIUM_CONFIDENCE_THRESHOLD = Fraction(3, 5)` (60%) [^9^]. CAIE, which operates in a domain requiring decimals, uses `decimal.Decimal` with fixed precision: `getcontext().prec = 28` and `ROUND_HALF_EVEN` rounding [^10^]. Every inference result includes a reproducible SHA-256 hash: `result_hash = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(result_dict, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()` [^11^]. Same input, same winning hypothesis, same hash on any machine.

### 3.3 Cross-Artifact Incongruence Engine (CAIE)

#### 3.3.1 Nine Forensic Fracture Rules (Golden Forensic Rules)

CAIE is the largest (~1,800 lines) and most complex module in the system. Designed by Kimi (Moonshot AI) and implemented by Claude (Anthropic), it detects logical fractures between evidence sources via 9 rules with documented severities. The `TEMPORAL_CAUSALITY_VIOLATION` rule carries the maximum severity (1.0) because an effect preceding its cause sequentially invalidates the entire inference chain. The `LOG_VS_MEMORY` (0.9) and `DOCUMENT_FORGERY` (0.9) rules identify the most frequent contradictions in anti-forensic cases, while `TIMESTAMP_PRECISION_ANOMALY` (0.95) specifically detects the signature of timestomping tools such as the Metasploit suite [^12^].

#### 3.3.2 17-Type Evidence Spoofability Table

CAIE assigns each evidence type a *spoofability* coefficient (the likelihood of being convincingly faked) and a weight reflecting its probative value. The matrix spans a range from 0.05 (cryptographically anchored evidence) to 0.90 (trivially modifiable network metadata).

| Evidence Type | Spoofability | Weight | Reason for Value |
|---|---|---|---|
| ip_geolocation | 0.90 | 0.15 | VPN/proxy anonymize origin with no local trace |
| cultural_marker | 0.90 | 0.15 | Language and keyboard layout are selectable |
| log_entry | 0.85 | 0.15 | Syslog/eventlog writable by administrators |
| user_agent | 0.85 | 0.15 | HTTP header modifiable on any request |
| file_timestamp | 0.70 | 0.20 | `touch` command or system APIs alter mtime/atime |
| registry_key | 0.55 | 0.20 | Windows Registry writable with elevated privileges |
| file_hash | 0.50 | 0.25 | SHA-256 verifies content but not context |
| prefetch | 0.25 | 0.28 | Managed by OS Superfetch; requires prior compromise |
| usn_journal | 0.20 | 0.30 | NTFS USN journal accessible only at kernel level |
| memory_process | 0.15 | 0.30 | Volatile memory requires runtime compromise |
| lsass_session | 0.15 | 0.30 | Cryptographically derived credentials |
| kernel_structure | 0.10 | 0.35 | EPROCESS/ETHREAD in kernel address space |
| digital_signature | 0.10 | 0.40 | PKI requires compromise of the CA's private key |
| timestamp_precision | 0.05 | 0.40 | Sub-second precision as a tool signature |
| hmac_audit_log | 0.05 | 0.40 | HMAC-chained log; requires the integrity key |
| hardware_serial | 0.05 | 0.40 | Serial numbers require physical device access |
| mft_entry | 0.05 | 0.42 | MFT entry number assigned by the NTFS driver |
| cryptographic_hash | 0.05 | 0.45 | Hash against known-good database; collision computationally infeasible |

The table reveals a forensic-trust hierarchy that doesn't match the traditional collection hierarchy. Investigators tend to prioritize event logs for their volume and accessibility, but these have a spoofability of 0.85, barely above network metadata. By contrast, kernel structures (`kernel_structure`, 0.10) and MFT records (`mft_entry`, 0.05) offer substantially higher trust even though extracting them requires specialized tools. CAIE functions as an implicit collection optimizer: by adjusting scores via `(1 - spoofability)`, it penalizes hypotheses supported mainly by low-falsification-cost evidence [^13^].

#### 3.3.3 Noisy-OR Model and Infinity Guard Against Score Poisoning

CAIE implements two protection mechanisms against adversarial scoring manipulation. The *Noisy-OR* model prevents *flood attacks* where a single tool generates multiple alerts to dominate the verdict: `group_score = 1 - prod(1 - score_i)` within each dependent-evidence group, and `composite = 1 - prod(1 - group_j)` across independent groups [^14^]. This model saturates the aggregate score as the number of correlated alerts grows, preventing 100 alerts from the same source from distorting the verdict. In complement, the *Infinity Guard* protects against *score poisoning*: every numeric value passes through `math.isfinite()` before being incorporated into the calculation. If an attacker injects `float('inf')`, `float('-inf')`, or `float('nan')`, the artifact is nullified and the system fires a `FORENSIC_POISONING_ATTEMPT` alert [^15^].

### 3.4 Devil's Advocate and the Validation System

#### 3.4.1 Deterministic Abductive Falsification Generation (R7)

The Devil's Advocate (rule R7) implements *Eco's Razor*: abductive falsification as a systematic counterweight to hypothesis generation. Approved by a VIGÍA Collective vote on June 19, 2026, its design deliberately excludes LLMs from the critical path [^16^]. The `compose_devil_advocate_struct()` composer operates in five steps: (1) it receives `pattern_signal_metadata` from the *CasePatternLibrary*; (2) it extracts missing signals and per-pattern match scores; (3) it ranks patterns by descending score and selects the *top-k* (k=3 by default) to preserve counterfactual diversity; (4) it computes `gap_strength = len(missing_signals) * pattern_score` for each pattern; (5) it generates a falsification narrative that explicitly explains which signals are missing and why the leading hypothesis could be wrong [^17^].

The `devil_advocate_source` field documents the provenance of each falsification in three mutually exclusive categories: `deterministic_missing_signals` (patterns matched identified gaps), `deterministic_no_pattern_data_available` (the *CasePatternLibrary* didn't run on this path), and `deterministic_no_pattern_matched` (no pattern matches the evidence) [^18^]. This taxonomy allows Devil's Advocate coverage to be audited per case.

The system has a documented limitation (L-025): on the standalone path (`vigia_scorer.py`), the `devil_advocate` field is only populated when a human curator writes it manually into the case JSON before building the corpus. No component of the autonomous pipeline generates this field at investigation time on that path [^19^]. The limitation does not affect the full agent mode (`vigia_agent.py` + `sift_orchestrator.py`), where the Devil's Advocate operates on *CasePatternLibrary* data.

#### 3.4.2 Intent Scale: NOISE/SUSPICION/INTENT/MALICE

VIGÍA defines an operationalized intent scale with four levels. Each level requires a strictly increasing set of conditions: NOISE (random patterns with no structural correlation), SUSPICION (anomalies requiring explanation), INTENT (anomalies with a minimum-cost abductive explanation), and MALICE (INTENT + Devil's Advocate survived + CAIE fracture confirmation). The *CollapseDecisionLayer* implements an aggressive policy: any break in `sensor_independence` forces the verdict to INCONCLUSIVE, prioritizing epistemic integrity over coverage [^20^].

#### 3.4.3 Four-State System with Fraction Thresholds

The `RiskBoundedDecisionLayer` defines four alert levels with exact-fraction thresholds, removing all ambiguity at the decision boundaries.

| Level | Threshold (Fraction) | Decimal Value | Verdict Issued | Override Condition |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| LOW | `< 15/100` | < 0.15 | NO_SEMIOTIC_ANOMALY_DETECTED | None |
| MEDIUM | `[15/100, 30/100)` | [0.15, 0.30) | ADVERSARIAL_SEMIOTIC_PATTERN_DETECTED | None |
| HIGH | `[30/100, 60/100)` | [0.30, 0.60) | ADVERSARIAL_SEMIOTIC_PATTERN_DETECTED | None |
| CRITICAL | `>= 60/100` | >= 0.60 | ADVERSARIAL_SEMIOTIC_PATTERN_DETECTED | ECO_SEMIOTIC_COLLISION forces CRITICAL |

Choosing `Fraction` over `float` is functional, not stylistic. Binary floating-point thresholds cannot exactly represent fractions like 15/100 (0.15 = 0.001001100110011... in binary), which introduces cross-platform variability. `Fraction(15, 100)` is exactly 3/20 on any architecture [^21^]. The `ECO_SEMIOTIC_COLLISION` override lets the decision layer automatically escalate to CRITICAL when the Devil's Advocate detects a semiotic collision: the coexistence of mutually exclusive patterns that no single hypothesis can explain, signaling with high probability a false-flag operation or advanced anti-forensics.

For finer-grained verdicts, the `QuadripartiteClassifier` expands the system to 8 states with two additional thresholds: `Fraction(4, 5)` (80%, high confidence) and `Fraction(3, 5)` (60%, medium confidence). The `ABSTAIN_CONTRADICTION`, `ABSTAIN_INSUFFICIENT`, and `ABSTAIN_DEGRADED` states formalize abstention as a valid verdict, not a system failure. As the calibration metadata states: "ABSTAIN on VIGIA-REAL cases is epistemologically correct: legacy artifacts have only 2 anomalies... with insufficient evidence, ABSTAIN is the honest, Daubert-defensible answer" [^22^]. In a field that traditionally rewards confidence over honesty, this abstention architecture constitutes a significant epistemological inversion.

## 4. Indicators of Intent: Beyond Traditional IOCs

Digital forensics has operated for decades under a reactive paradigm: the analyst finds a malicious hash, a suspicious IP, or a fraudulent domain and searches for matches across compromised systems. This model, based on *Indicators of Compromise* (IOCs), answers one basic question: **"what happened?"** However, the 2025–2026 threat landscape has eroded the effectiveness of this approach. 82% of the detections CrowdStrike reported in 2025 were *malware-free* — meaning they left no detectable static artifacts [^838^]. EDR-evasion tools sell on underground forums for as little as $300 [^782^], and average *breakout time* has dropped to 29 minutes [^836^]. In this context, detecting *what* happened is no longer enough: it's necessary to infer *why* it happened and *who benefits* from the investigator adopting a particular interpretation.

VIGÍA addresses this gap through an *Indicators of Intent* (IoI) framework that represents an epistemological leap in DFIR (*Digital Forensics and Incident Response*): the shift from detecting technical artifacts to detecting deliberate intent [^3^].

### 4.1 The Indicator Hierarchy: From IOCs to IoIs

The cybersecurity ecosystem has evolved through three generations of indicators, each representing a higher level of abstraction and interpretation. The table below synthesizes this hierarchy:

| Dimension | IOC (Indicator of Compromise) | IOA (Indicator of Attack) | IoI (Indicator of Intent) |
|-----------|------------------------------|---------------------------|---------------------------|
| **Focus** | Evidence after the attack | Behavior during the attack | Intent behind the behavior |
| **Temporality** | Reactive | Proactive | Interpretive-abductive |
| **Nature** | Static (hashes, IPs, domains) | Dynamic (TTPs) | Semiotic (signs of deliberation) |
| **Central question** | "What happened?" | "How did they do it?" | "Who benefits from this interpretation?" |
| **Detection basis** | Known signatures | Tactics, techniques, and procedures | Fractures in communicative coherence |
| **Theoretical foundation** | Pattern matching | MITRE ATT&CK + ML | Peircean semiotics + Gricean pragmatics |
| **Operation in VIGÍA** | Firstness input | Hypothesis template | Abductive engine + CAIE |

*Sources: CrowdStrike [^8^]; SISA [^366^]; Forsythe [^7^]; VIGÍA [^3^]*

The distinction isn't merely technical — it's epistemological. While IOCs operate at the Peircean level of *Secondness* (correlation between observed artifacts), IoIs operate at the level of *Thirdness*: the inferred law or habit that explains a deliberate pattern [^3^]. CrowdStrike introduced *Indicators of Attack* (IOAs) in 2012 to detect real-time behavior [^8^]. SISA proposed *Indicators of Behavior* (IoB) in 2022 as "behavioral particles that determine the context and intent of a threat" [^366^]. VIGÍA completes this ladder: IoIs analyze not the behavior itself, but the intent that motivates it.

This leap answers the Latin legal principle *Cui bono?* ("who benefits?"), operationalized through inference to the best explanation [^418^][^30^]. The question VIGÍA poses for every piece of evidence isn't just "what happened here?" but "who wins if the investigator believes this was a mistake?" [^3^].

### 4.2 VIGÍA's Five Indicators of Intent

VIGÍA defines five IoIs grounded in linguistic pragmatics, semiotics, and forensic science. Each detects a specific pattern of intentional manipulation.

**Weaponized Incompetence.** This IoI detects when an actor deliberately fakes technical incompetence to conceal malicious activity. Case **CAN-031** documents the pattern with precision: PowerShell runs flawless commands to delete *shadow copies* and disable the firewall — zero syntax errors — and 63 seconds later the same user files an IT ticket complaining that "my screen flickered, I'm useless with computers" [^853^]. The absence of errors in destructive commands contradicts the incompetence narrative. The detection rests on the violation of Grice's Quality and Quantity maxims [^9^][^21^] and on McCornack's *Information Manipulation Theory 2*: lies are built from manipulated truths to induce a false conclusion [^24^].

**Excessive Digital Perfection.** Real computer systems are inherently noisy: they produce minor errors, timestamp variability, duplicate logs, and debug events. An artifact that's "too clean" — lacking these natural imperfections — is a sign of deliberate intervention. Case **CAN-018** encapsulates this principle: 847 commands executed at exactly 300,000-second intervals, zero errors, zero retries, 0.00 bits of temporal entropy [^853^]. Such perfection is statistically impossible on a real operating system. Technically, this IoI connects to the anti-forensic category of *trail obfuscation* documented by Rogers and Conlan [^118^][^444^]. VIGÍA's CAIE **DOCUMENT_FORGERY** rule fires at severity 0.9 when it detects this anomaly [^26^].

**Significant Silences.** The absence of artifacts that should be present can be as revealing as their presence. This is *evidence whose absence is evidence of intent*. William C. Thompson et al. formally demonstrated, via Bayesian inference, that the absence of evidence DOES constitute evidence of absence when three conditions hold: the search was adequate, the evidence should be present given the context, and the absence favors one hypothesis over another [^449^]. VIGÍA detects significant silences via CAIE's **USN_JOURNAL_GAP** rule, which identifies gaps in the NTFS USN Journal — a system artifact that rarely shows natural gaps [^26^]. In Gricean pragmatic terms, a significant silence violates the Quantity maxim: "make your contribution as informative as is required" [^9^].

**Impossible Timing.** This IoI detects temporal inconsistencies that cannot occur naturally: an effect before its cause, timestamps with precision impossible for the system, or sequences that violate the physical laws of computation. *Timestomping* — timestamp manipulation — is the most documented anti-forensic technique, used by dozens of APT groups including Lazarus, APT28, and APT29 [^768^]. VIGÍA implements the **TEMPORAL_CAUSALITY_VIOLATION** rule with maximum severity (1.0), which directly detects an "effect before cause" [^26^]. The **TIMESTAMP_PRECISION_ANOMALY** rule (severity 0.95) identifies sub-seconds truncated to zero, a characteristic timestomping signature [^26^]. The TER model (*Timeline based Event Reconstruction*, 2025) provides the theoretical grounding for this detection [^417^][^393^].

**Narrative Fractures.** When multiple artifacts should tell the same story but don't, a narrative fracture results. Brookman et al. (2020) showed that forensic narratives integrate character, motive, intent, and chronology; when artifacts give contradictory versions of these elements, the narrative fractures [^419^]. VIGÍA's **CAIE** (*Cross-Artifact Incongruence Engine*) detects these fractures via nine specific rules [^26^]. The **LOG_VS_MEMORY** rule (0.9) fires when "the logs say X, but memory says it didn't happen." The **NETWORK_VS_HOST** rule (0.8) fires when the firewall logs traffic but the host has no open sockets. The **FALSE_FLAG_PATTERN** rule (0.8) identifies "high cultural markers + zero technical corroboration" — the classic false-flag pattern [^26^]. Each fracture raises the computational cost of maintaining a coherent lie, making deception progressively more expensive for the attacker.

### 4.3 Detecting Fabricated Artifacts and False Flags

*False flags* — deliberate deception in which threat actors disguise their identity — represent one of the most demanding applications of IoIs. Documented cases include *Olympic Destroyer* (2018), where Russia attributed the attack to North Korea [^783^], and the *DNC Hack* (2016), where GRU operators posed as a lone Romanian hacker [^783^].

VIGÍA includes specific *false-flag* cases in its evaluation corpus: 3 of 3 genuine false flags were correctly detected [^853^]. The detection mechanism works through CAIE looking for incongruities among artifacts that should corroborate each other but don't. When an attacker copies the TTPs of a known group but makes mistakes that group wouldn't make — or plants cultural markers with no technical backing — the system detects the fracture. Case **L-019** (cultural-attribution false flag) was correctly resolved, demonstrating that adversarial abduction, conceptualized by Forsythe as "semiotic efforts to mislead an adversary's abductions" [^7^], can be operationalized computationally.

The relevance of this capability grows with the sophistication of threat actors. When 82% of detections are *malware-free* [^838^] and *living-off-the-land* techniques appear in 84% of high-severity attacks [^761^], the only remaining signal is often the intentional inconsistency — the mark the attacker can't remove without leaving another mark. VIGÍA quantifies this fracture: CAIE's adjusted-scoring formula, $adjusted\_score = raw\_score \times (1 - spoofability) \times weight$, mathematically penalizes high-falsifiability artifacts, revealing the fractures that signal deliberate manipulation [^26^]. This mechanism transforms the economics of digital deception: while lying in a log or fabricating an attack has traditionally been computationally cheap, VIGÍA raises the cost of the lie by demanding perfect coherence across multiple layers of evidence simultaneously. An attacker who can fake a log (easy) must now also fake memory (hard), timestamps (very hard), and cross-artifact correlations (nearly impossible). VIGÍA's IoIs don't replace IOCs and IOAs — they complement them, adding an interpretive layer that asks, for every artifact, whether the story it tells is what actually happened — or what someone wants the investigator to believe.

## 5. Security, LLM Isolation, and Chain of Custody

### 5.1 Isolation Architecture: LLMs Outside the Verdict Path

#### 5.1.1 Fundamental Principle: Verdict Sealed Before the LLM Sees the Evidence

VIGÍA's security architecture is built on a non-negotiable premise: the forensic verdict is computed and cryptographically sealed before any language model (LLM, *Large Language Model*) has access to the evidence. This principle responds to a structural vulnerability documented in AI systems applied to forensics: LLMs, even operating with deterministic parameters, exhibit residual variance sufficient to alter interpretations in high-uncertainty contexts. The VIGÍA corpus's BREAK-012 case demonstrates this fragility: the Claude model incorrectly flipped a verdict from BENIGN to MALICE, an event classified as a model hallucination [^263^].

VIGÍA implements a strict architectural separation between the deterministic inference engine and narrative LLMs. The data flow follows a unidirectional topology: raw evidence enters the deterministic engine (Layers 0–3), which produces a sealed bundle (EBS v1); only after sealing can the bundle — now immutable — be passed to the narrative pipeline for report generation. The LLM never participates in computing the *z-score*, building the evidence graph, or making the ACCEPT/REJECT/ABSTAIN decision [^295^].

#### 5.1.2 BundleBuilder as an External Process: A Compromised Engine Can't Seal Its Own Lie

Cryptographic sealing doesn't live in the inference engine but in `bundle_builder.py`, an external attestation process. This design decision, audited by Gemini and DeepSeek, answers a fundamental security argument: *a bundle that hashes itself lets a compromised engine seal its own lie* [^324^]. By externalizing sealing, VIGÍA guarantees that neither a malicious modification of the engine nor a runtime injection can produce an apparently valid bundle without an independent verifier detecting it.

The full architecture is organized into five cumulative security layers:

| Layer | Component | Security Function | Cryptographic Primitive |
|------|-----------|----------------------|------------------------|
| 0 — Immutable data | EBS v1 (`ebs_v1.py`) | Pure data specification; no business logic, no LLM references | None (raw data) |
| 1 — Chained integrity | BundleBuilder (`bundle_builder.py`) | External attestation; 5-step hashing protocol | Chained SHA-256 |
| 2 — Independent verification | `verify_ebs_v1.py` | Third-party audit with no production dependencies | SHA-256 (stdlib only) |
| 3 — Forensic custody | HMAC Audit Logger | Sequential record with forward integrity | Chained HMAC-SHA256 |
| 4 — Runtime governance | ConfigSentinel + Sandbox | Degradation detection; process containment | HMAC-SHA256 + `setrlimit` |

Each layer compensates for the others' potential weaknesses. Layer 0 guarantees that data is interpretable without production code; Layer 1 ensures the engine can't self-validate tampering; Layer 2 lets any third party with Python 3.6+ verify a bundle; Layer 3 creates a cryptographic *ratchet* where altering any entry invalidates the entire subsequent chain; and Layer 4 protects against silent degradation of critical modules and runtime privilege escalation [^295^] [^324^] [^316^].

### 5.2 Evidence Bundle Standard v1 (EBS v1)

#### 5.2.1 Layer 0: Pure, Immutable Data — No Business Logic, No LLM References

The Evidence Bundle Standard v1 is VIGÍA's forensic data specification, implemented in `ebs_v1.py` (801 lines, 29.1 KB) [^295^]. The absolute rule governing this module is documented explicitly in the source code: *"ABSOLUTE RULE: This module contains DATA ONLY. No business logic. No hashing. No sealing. No references to LLMs, Ollama, or narrative backends."* This separation isn't merely organizational — it's a guarantee that the evidence format remains interpretable regardless of the system that produced it or the language model that later narrates it.

The main container, `ForensicBundle`, groups six components: `EvidenceGraph` (dependency graph among artifacts), `DecisionTrace` (decision trace with *posterior*, *risk*, and *log-likelihood ratio*), `PolicySpec` (runtime-independent policy specification), a list of suggested actions, system state, and the abduction trace (`AbductionTrace`). None of these components execute code or call hashing functions; the `integrity` field, of type `IntegrityBlock`, is assigned exclusively by the external `BundleBuilder` process [^295^].

#### 5.2.2 Invariants I1–I5: Determinism, Chained Integrity, Verifiable Policy

The standard defines five invariants every valid bundle must satisfy. I1 (*Determinism*) states that the same input produces a bit-identical bundle, regardless of hardware architecture or Python interpreter version. I2 (*Chained integrity*) requires that `bundle_hash` cover the entire payload content. I3 (*Verifiable policy*) guarantees that the decision policy is independent of the runtime environment running the analysis. I4 (*Explicit actions*) forbids implicit side effects: every suggested action must be explicitly declared. I5 (*Explainable decision*) requires the `risk` and `posterior` fields to always be present in the decision trace [^295^].

Satisfying these invariants enables a critical forensic property: intersubjective reproducibility. Any analyst, on any machine, can reconstruct the reasoning that led to the verdict from the bundle alone, with no access to the system that generated it.

#### 5.2.3 Independent Verifier: stdlib-Only Python, Zero Production Imports

`verify_ebs_v1.py` (309 lines) implements the standard's independent verifier. Its independence guarantee is total: it uses exclusively Python's standard library, importing no class from VIGÍA's production code [^316^]. The standard's constants — supported version, required field names, validation thresholds — are deliberately copied into the verifier rather than imported from `ebs_v1.py`. As the module's documentation states: *"If the verifier needs to import production code, the system is not third-party-auditable — it violates the forensic independence principle"* [^316^].

The verifier implements six validation rules across three severity levels (ERROR, WARNING, CRITICAL) and four conformance levels, from Level 0 (*Non-compliant*) to Level 3 (*Fully compliant EBS v1*). Rule R6 (*Devil's Advocate*) is the only one classified as CRITICAL: a MALICE or INTENT verdict that hasn't passed devil's-advocate validation triggers immediate verification failure [^316^].

### 5.3 Cryptographic Chain of Custody

#### 5.3.1 Chained HMAC-SHA256 with Forward Integrity

The chain-of-custody system implements a *forward integrity* scheme using chained HMAC-SHA256. Each audit-log entry holds two cryptographic fields: `_prev_hmac`, storing the HMAC of the previous entry (or the "GENESIS" string for the first one), and `_hmac`, computing the HMAC-SHA256 of the entry's content concatenated with `_prev_hmac` [^263^]. This structure creates a robust security property: altering any line invalidates every subsequent entry, since each `_hmac` cryptographically depends on the previous one. Full-chain verification is performed via `audit_logger.verify_chain()`, which sequentially walks the log validating each link [^263^].

HMAC key resolution follows a three-tier hierarchy: the `VIGIA_HMAC_KEY` environment variable (hex-encoded, minimum 32 bytes), an external file via `VIGIA_HMAC_KEY_FILE`, or automatic ephemeral generation — the latter only in development environments, logged as a WARNING. The ephemeral key has a known limitation: when the process restarts, the key is lost and the prior chain can't be verified [^263^].

#### 5.3.2 5-Step Protocol: graph_hash → policy_hash → decision_hash → bundle_hash

The BundleBuilder's hashing protocol runs in five sequential steps that accumulate cryptographic integrity from individual components up to the full bundle [^324^]:

Step 1: *graph_hash* = SHA-256 of the evidence graph **without** the `graph_hash` field.

Step 2: *policy_hash* = SHA-256 of the policy specification **without** the `created_at` field (guaranteeing temporal reproducibility).

Step 3: *decision_hash* = SHA-256 of the complete decision trace.

Step 4: the graph is updated with the assigned `graph_hash` → `graph_dict_final`.

Step 5: *bundle_hash* = SHA-256 of the canonical concatenation of `bundle_id`, `version`, `timestamp`, `graph_dict_final`, `decision_trace`, `policy_spec`, `actions`, and `system_state`.

Strict canonicalization (designated H22 in the internal documentation) solves a cross-platform determinism problem: JSON doesn't distinguish `int(1)` from `float(1.0)`. The `_canonicalize()` function transforms types unambiguously — `float` to a string with 8 fixed decimals, `int` to a string with an `:int` suffix, `bool` to lowercase `"true"`/`"false"`, `None` to `"null"`, and dictionaries with lexicographically sorted keys — guaranteeing the bundle hash is identical on any platform [^324^].

#### 5.3.3 Witness Mode with Human Co-Signature (DUAL_CUSTODY/UNSIGNED/HARD_FAIL)

For critical verdicts (MALICE or INTENT), VIGÍA implements *Witness Mode*: an HMAC-SHA256 co-signature with the human operator's key (`VIGIA_HUMAN_OPERATOR_KEY`), creating a *dual-custody* scheme where one key derives from the audit log's HMAC chain and the other belongs to the qualified analyst [^263^]. The system operates in three mutually exclusive modes:

In `DUAL_CUSTODY` mode, the operator key is present and the report is co-signed; the verdict reaches *Daubert-admissible* status. In `UNSIGNED` mode, the key is absent but the system generates a *soft warning*; the bundle is usable but lacks human certification. In `HARD_FAIL` mode, triggered when `VIGIA_FORENSIC_STRICT=true` and the operator key is absent, the verdict is invalidated and the investigation aborts, logging the `WITNESS_HARD_FAIL` event at CRITICAL severity in the audit log. The operator key must be at least 32 characters; weak keys are also rejected in strict mode [^263^].

### 5.4 Sandbox and Governance

#### 5.4.1 Sandbox with setrlimit and Privilege Dropping

The `vigia/security/sandbox.py` module (~400 lines) implements process containment via the `sandboxed_execute()` wrapper, which invokes `asyncio.create_subprocess_exec` with POSIX restrictions imposed via `setrlimit` [^305^]. The default limits are: 512 MB virtual memory (`RLIMIT_AS`), 30 seconds of CPU time (`RLIMIT_CPU`), zero core dumps (`RLIMIT_CORE = (0, 0)`), 50 MB file size (`RLIMIT_FSIZE`), 1,024 open files (`RLIMIT_NOFILE`), 64 MB stack (`RLIMIT_STACK`), and 64 processes (`RLIMIT_NPROC`) [^305^].

The system implements conditional privilege dropping: if the `VIGIA_DROP_PRIVS_UID` variable is set and the process is running as root, it switches to the specified UID before running the subprocess. If `setuid()` fails, the process aborts with `os._exit(126)` — it never continues with elevated privileges [^305^]. On Windows, behavior is fail-safe: if `VIGIA_ENFORCE_POSIX_SANDBOX=true` on a non-POSIX platform, the system aborts at startup; without enforcement, it applies an aggressive 5-second timeout.

#### 5.4.2 ConfigSentinel: Detecting Degradation of Critical Modules

`config_sentinel.py` (~240 lines) acts as a runtime integrity guardian for the system. It monitors a set of critical modules — CAIE (*Cross-Artifact Incongruence Engine*), TrustFusion, OckhamAdversarial, and SignalRouter — and detects three degradation patterns: deactivation of critical modules at startup, runtime configuration changes (*tampering*), and silent degradation induced by environment variables [^298^].

The operating flow has three phases: `initialize()` captures a cryptographic *snapshot* of the configuration before analysis begins; `checkpoint()` checks for changes against the baseline between pipeline phases; and `finalize()` closes the audit *trail*. Each degradation event is sealed with HMAC-SHA256 using the monitor's secret key. If a critical module is disabled during analysis, the system fires a `ConfigurationTamperedException`, interrupting the pipeline [^298^].

VIGÍA's security architecture has gone through multiple audit rounds by Kimi (Moonshot), Gemini (Google), and DeepSeek, with 16+ documented security fixes in the repository, including MCP transport vulnerabilities (V-002), rate limiting (V-003), symlink validation (V-004), and signal sanitization before LLM ingestion [^263^]. This multi-party auditing, combined with Apache 2.0 open-source licensing, constitutes a structural advantage over black-box forensic tools whose evidence has been excluded from courts for lack of transparency [^245^].

## 6. Computational Determinism and Daubert Standard Compliance

### 6.1 The Floating-Point Problem in Forensics

#### 6.1.1 Non-Associativity and Non-Determinism of Parallel Computation

IEEE-754 floating-point arithmetic has a property that disqualifies it for legal forensic applications: **it is not associative**. In other words, $(a + b) + c$ doesn't necessarily equal $a + (b + c)$ [^611^]. In parallel computing — including GPU computation — evaluation order depends on the thread scheduler, which is inherently non-deterministic. A 2024 study showed that variability from non-associativity in parallel GPU operations reaches the tolerance thresholds of high-precision molecular simulation [^683^]. Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory documented order-of-magnitude differences in rounding errors between different reduction operations on accelerators [^681^]. NVIDIA classifies the determinism of its GPUs into three levels: *not-guaranteed*, *run-to-run*, and identical *gpu-to-gpu* — the latter carrying a 20–30% performance penalty [^679^]. In forensics, a bit that flips at bit 52 of the mantissa can change a verdict from SUSPICION to MALICE, invalidate a bundle's SHA-256 hash, or produce different conclusions on different machines.

#### 6.1.2 Historical Cases: Intel Pentium FDIV ($475M), Patriot Missile (28 dead), Ariane 5 ($370M)

The literature documents three paradigmatic disasters caused by numerical-representation errors. The **Intel Pentium FDIV bug (1994)** — five missing entries in a table of 1,066 — produced incorrect divisions with a probability of 1 in 9 billion, costing Intel $475 million in replacements, plus class-action lawsuits and an SEC investigation [^695^] [^696^] [^697^]. The **Patriot Missile failure (1991)** was more tragic: the value 0.1 seconds — not terminating in binary — was truncated to 24 bits; after 100 hours, the accumulated error reached ~0.34 seconds, enough for a Scud traveling at 1,676 m/s to travel ~570 meters outside the *range gate*, killing 28 soldiers in Dhahran [^705^] [^709^] [^710^] [^711^]. **Ariane 5 Flight 501 (1996)** self-destructed when horizontal velocity exceeded 32,767 — the int16 maximum — during a float64-to-integer conversion, destroying $370 million plus a $500 million payload [^708^] [^713^] [^715^] [^716^] [^719^]. Three distinct mechanisms — a hardware table, rounding accumulation, type overflow — converge on the same lesson: a system that doesn't control its numerical arithmetic cannot guarantee the integrity of its conclusions.

### 6.2 Exact Arithmetic in VIGÍA

#### 6.2.1 Python `fractions.Fraction` for Decision Thresholds

VIGÍA completely avoids IEEE-754 floating point in its decision layer. The thresholds separating the four verdict levels are defined using `fractions.Fraction`, which represents exact rational numbers as (numerator, denominator) pairs of arbitrary-precision integers [^152^]. In `vigia_scorer.py`:

```python
elif final_score > Fraction(3, 4):     # exactly 0.75
    verdict = "MALICE"
elif final_score > Fraction(11, 20):  # exactly 0.55
    verdict = "SUSPICION"
elif final_score > Fraction(1, 4):    # exactly 0.25
    verdict = "UNKNOWN"
```

With `float(0.75)`, a score of `0.7500000000000001` — the product of accumulated rounding errors — would incorrectly cross the threshold. With `Fraction(3, 4)`, that scenario is mathematically impossible.

#### 6.2.2 `decimal.Decimal(prec=28)` for Intermediate Computation

For intermediate computation — cumulative sums, normalizations — VIGÍA uses `decimal.Decimal` with fixed 28-digit precision and `ROUND_HALF_EVEN` rounding, eliminating the bit-52 divergence that native `round()` produces between x86-64 and ARM64 architectures [^152^]. The `_dround()` and `_dsum()` functions act as "finite-math shields": faced with `inf`, `-inf`, or `NaN` values, they return 0.0, preventing corrupted artifacts from propagating toxicity into the verdict.

#### 6.2.3 Guarantee: "Same Input → Same SHA-256 Bundle Hash on Any Machine, Any Run"

The architecture operates in three layers: `fractions.Fraction` for exact thresholds, `decimal.Decimal` for controlled-precision computation, and SHA-256 for cryptographic sealing. Every `ForensicRecord` generates its hash via `json.dumps(sort_keys=True, ensure_ascii=False)` followed by SHA-256, guaranteeing deterministic serialization. The system is *stateless* by design: no random seeds, no network calls, no timestamps in the decision hash. This bit-exact reproducibility guarantee is a necessary condition that NIST SP 800-86 sets for the admissibility of electronic evidence: *repeatable* and *reproducible* results [^680^].

| Property | `float` (IEEE-754) | `fractions.Fraction` | Forensic Implication |
|---|---|---|---|
| Representation | 53-bit mantissa (approximate) | (num, den) pair of unlimited integers (exact) | `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` is `False` with `float`; `True` with `Fraction` |
| Associativity | No: $(a+b)+c \neq a+(b+c)$ | Yes | `Fraction` produces the same result regardless of evaluation order |
| Cross-platform hash | Not guaranteed | Guaranteed | `Fraction` produces the same hash on x86-64, ARM64, or any platform |
| Serialization | `repr()` can vary across platforms | `repr()` always exact | `Fraction` is reproducible on deserialization |
| Performance penalty | ~1 CPU cycle | ~50–500× slower | Acceptable for forensic scoring (dozens of artifacts, not millions of operations) |
| Determinism on parallel GPU | No (scheduler non-associativity) | Yes | `Fraction` eliminates the source of non-determinism in parallel computation |

### 6.3 Daubert Standard Compliance

#### 6.3.1 The 5 Daubert Factors and How VIGÍA Meets Them

The *Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals, Inc.*, 509 U.S. 579 (1993), standard imposes a gatekeeping obligation on the judge: ensuring expert testimony "rests on a reliable foundation and is relevant" [^145^] [^161^]. The Court formulated five indicative factors, later extended by *Kumho Tire Co. v. Carmichael*, 526 U.S. 137 (1999), to **all** expert testimony [^162^].

| Daubert Factor | Requirement | VIGÍA Implementation | Verifiable Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Testability (falsifiability) | The method can be tested empirically | `VIGIA_FORENSIC_LOCK=true`; `fractions.Fraction`; fixed seed | `make check-determinism` runs $N$ times and compares SHA-256 hashes |
| 2. Peer review | Method subjected to review and publication | Apache 2.0 open source on public GitHub | Any expert can audit the code; `verify_ebs_v1.py` uses stdlib only [^184^] |
| 3. Known error rate | Documented error rate | 4-level scale; `what_would_falsify_this` field | FPR, FNR-MAL, TTP Coverage metrics; 55/55 EBS v1 tests |
| 4. Standards and controls | Standards governing operation | P2 Protocol; ISO 27037:2012; NIST SP 800-86 | `_dround()` with fixed precision; HMAC-SHA256 chain |
| 5. General acceptance | Acceptance in the relevant community | SANS FIND EVIL 2026; STIX 2.1; MITRE ATT&CK | Widely accepted exchange formats |

A non-deterministic method **cannot** have a known error rate because its results vary between runs [^589^]. If a score changes between machines due to floating-point differences, the system isn't *repeatable*, its error rate is incalculable, and it's inadmissible under Daubert. VIGÍA solves this problem at its arithmetic root.

#### 6.3.2 FRE 702 (2023 Amendment): The New "More Likely Than Not" Requirement

The amendment to Rule 702, effective December 1, 2023, introduces two fundamental changes [^143^] [^147^]. First, the proponent must show by a preponderance of the evidence ("more likely than not") that the testimony meets **all** the requirements; previously, many courts treated methodology as going to "weight" for the jury rather than admissibility [^591^]. Second, the expert's opinion must reflect "a reliable application of the principles and methods to the facts of the case." The Advisory Committee instructed that forensic examiners "should avoid assertions of absolute certainty" [^147^]. VIGÍA satisfies this through its 4-level system, which avoids absolute binary verdicts, and the `what_would_falsify_this` field, which documents the falsifiability conditions of every conclusion.

#### 6.3.3 FRE 902(13)/(14): Self-Authentication of Digital Evidence

The 2017 amendments created electronic self-authentication mechanisms [^180^] [^182^]. Rule 902(14) allows data from electronic devices to be authenticated through a "process of digital identification" — typically hash values — without live testimony. The Federal Judicial Center notes that "identical hash values for the original and the copy reliably attest that they are exact duplicates" [^182^]. VIGÍA implements atomic SHA-256 on read (`O_NOFOLLOW` + `os.fstat(fd)`), chained HMAC-SHA256 with `_prev_hmac`, read-only Docker mounting, and WORM via `chattr +i`, simultaneously satisfying ISO/IEC 27037:2012 [^707^].

#### 6.3.4 The Cybercheck Case: Why Black Boxes Fail in Court

The most illustrative contrast is provided by **Cybercheck**, AI software that claims to identify perpetrators with "90% accuracy" [^597^]. Its creator, Adam Mosher, refused to explain how it works; under oath he testified that Cybercheck **keeps no records** of where it gets data or how it computes its accuracy rates [^597^]. Judges in Colorado ruled its evidence inadmissible; in April 2024, lawyers in Ohio accused Mosher of perjury [^197^]. Facial recognition was excluded in 2025 for "reliability and transparency failures" [^197^]; in *Commonwealth v. Arrington*, 226 N.E.3d 851 (Mass. 2024), the Court excluded iPhone data because the algorithm was "proprietary and jealously guarded by Apple" [^613^] [^648^]. The lesson is unambiguous: **access to the algorithm is fundamental to admissibility**. VIGÍA removes this obstacle by design — its open-source code lets any opposing expert examine and verify every line. As Brian Carrier argued, open-source forensic tools enjoy "implicit community acceptance by virtue of their continued development and use," which has led to open-source forensics being called **"the digital Daubert standard"** [^184^].

## 7. Empirical Evaluation and Real-World Cases

Validating a forensic system requires confronting it with public datasets, verifiable ground truth, and scenarios that exercise every layer of the inference engine. VIGÍA has been subjected to three layers of evaluation — real corpus, canonical corpus, and structural tests — across a total of 125 cases and 55 automated tests. This chapter documents the quantitative results, the evaluation methodology, and three cases that illustrate how the system operates when intent is concealed behind sophisticated anti-forensic techniques.

### 7.1 Datasets and Evaluation Methodology

#### 7.1.1 Verified Public Datasets

VIGÍA uses six internationally recognized forensic-dataset sources: NIST CFReDS (*Computer Forensic Reference Data Sets*), developed by the IT Laboratory of the National Institute of Standards and Technology [^76^][^523^]; the DFRWS Forensic Challenges, run annually since 2005 with published solutions [^542^]; Digital Corpora, maintained by Simson Garfinkel, with scenarios such as Nitroba University and M57-Patents [^554^][^84^]; the SANS FOR508 course (Stark Research Labs 2018) [^548^][^549^]; Ali Hadi's datasets; and the Volatility Project's Cridex Banking Trojan. All meet three criteria: publicly verifiable ground truth, multiple artifact categories (disk, memory, network), and recognition within the DFIR community as a reference for tool evaluation.

#### 7.1.2 Canonical Corpus VIGIA-CAN

The canonical corpus comprises 52 synthetic cases with known ground truth, covering patterns documented in the anti-forensic literature: *weaponized incompetence*, *process hollowing*, *log ventriloquism*, phantom persistence, and cultural false flags. Each case runs via `tests/run_all_cases.py` (the deterministic Python pipeline, through `run_vigia_case.py` — not the autonomous agent), producing a `ForensicBundle` sealed with SHA-256 and an HMAC chain. Result: 52/52 correct (100%) in **Python mode**.

> **2026-06-22 correction:** the original version of this report attributed this result to "agent mode." Verification against the live repository confirmed that `run_all_cases.py` calls `run_vigia_case.py` (the deterministic scorer), never touching `vigia_agent.py`. The real autonomous-agent-mode metric is documented in §7.1.4.

#### 7.1.3 Real Corpus

The full regression suite, run via `run_all_agent.py` against `vigia_agent.py` (autonomous agent mode, not the standalone Python scorer), covers 136 cases spread across three evaluation domains:
